questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the two anchor bins (8 and 17) have unusually high gc_content compared with the other bins, and that contact counts depend on GC in every replicate. Check whether that holds in your data, and whether any dependence of your balanced values on the GC of the two bins remains after ICE (for example among the diagonal-9 pixels you average for the expected). Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team observed that ICE balancing on this truncated 24-bin window can be distorted by edge bins (which see only part of their contacts) and by the loop pixel's own contribution to the coverage of bins 8 and 17. Check in your data how the balancing weights of bins 8 and 17 and of the edge bins compare with the rest, and whether those weights change if the target pixel is left out of the balancing. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team left the target pixel (8,17) out of the data used to build the expected, whereas your primary expected is the diagonal-9 mean with that pixel included among only 11 valid pixels. You recorded that your result moves when the target is left out. Check how much of the diagonal-9 mean in each replicate comes from the target pixel itself, and state which definition of 'expected' you judge the task to mean and why. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that only 11 valid pixels remain on diagonal 9 once bins 10 and 11 are masked, that the result moves with how the diagonal-9 expected is defined (mean, median, target left out, smoothed across distances), that the distance-decay slope differs between case and control, and that control replicates have zero pixels at long range. Check whether these hold in your data, how many pixels actually determine the distance-9 factor in your GLM, and whether the long-range zeros or the differing decay affect the fit. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team corrected per-bin bias by balancing each replicate rather than with a single covariate, and found that bin coverage is strongly related to mappability, driven by bins 10 and 11. Your GC effect is one linear coefficient shared across all distances and fit on about 250 pixels. Check whether that coefficient is stable when it is estimated without the influence of particular bins (for example the edge bins or bins neighbouring 10 and 11), whether it is separable from mappability and re_sites in these 24 bins, and whether residual per-bin bias remains at bins 8 and 17 after your model. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team used two cross-checks you did not record: a local (donut) background around pixel (8,17) to tell a focal loop from broader domain enrichment, and the 40 kb pixel covering the same coordinates as a consistency check on the 20 kb estimate. Check whether your expected and your per-condition values are consistent with those two views in your data. Also state whether you judge that the task's 'expected' should include or exclude the target pixel, and why. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both teams mask bins 10/11, use per-replicate expected from the other 10 valid diagonal-9 pixels (target left out), and average log2 O/E per condition. The only difference is the bias model: X uses per-bin ICE visibility factors (target pixel excluded from balancing), giving 1.93/-0.29/2.22; Y uses an NB GLM with distance factors plus one summed-anchor-GC covariate, giving 1.84/-0.15/1.98.
referee.test: test.py: in each replicate, fit an NB GLM (alpha 0.05) on dist>=2 pixels without masked bins and without the target. Model A has diagonal factors plus GC-sum (Y). Model B has diagonal factors plus per-bin factors (X/ICE-equivalent). Held out each non-target pixel in anchor rows 8 and 17 (dist 2-15, 136 pixels over 4 reps) one at a time, predicted it, and compared NB deviance with a paired sign-flip permutation test. Also compared AIC and the target O/E under each model.
referee.reason: The disagreement comes entirely from choosing between two defensible bias corrections. The held-out test slightly favours GC-only in the controls, but not significantly, and the case replicates do not separate the models. The data cannot settle which bias correction is right, so neither answer is shown to be better. Both agree on a focal case-specific loop: delta about 2.0-2.2, case about 1.8-1.9, control about -0.15 to -0.3.

studies.title: Natural selection from allele frequencies over time

shared_assumptions: Both teams split the 0.16 seq_error into C->T 0.31 and T->C 0.01 and treat that split as fixed and known. It is inferred, not given, and both justify it with the same sentence: that locus A gen 6 (36/40 = 0.90) is 'impossible' under symmetric 0.16 because the ceiling is 0.84. That is a point comparison with no sampling noise: for 40 reads at a true rate of 0.84, P(X >= 36) is about 0.21, so this single sample does not by itself exclude the symmetric model. The remaining support is a non-nested log-likelihood gap of about 4 at locus A only (-30.0 vs -34.1); neither team reported the gap at locus B, jointly, or without the gen-6 sample.
Both assume the split is identical at the two loci and constant across all samples spanning 2000 years of sample age, because the seq_error column is constant.

Both assume a single constant s over generations 6-60. Under the asymmetric model the T-read floor is 0.31 and locus A's late T fractions (0.33-0.45) sit on or just above it, so the late derived frequencies, and therefore how much of the trajectory is 'saturated', are set almost entirely by the assumed floor rather than by the data.

Both use the N column as the haploid Wright-Fisher population size (drift variance p(1-p)/N) and neither records how the hidden chain is initialised (start at generation 0 or at the first sample at generation 6; prior on starting frequency). Neither reports sensitivity to these.

Both treat the two loci as independent (separate per-locus fits). In a haploid population the loci may be linked; the read depths are identical at every time point and the gen-12 counts are identical (34/45), so the two series come from the same samples. Not testable with strength from 9 points, but untested.
Both accept outgroup parsimony for polarisation (outgroup = T = alt at both loci), which also happens to be the allele that C->T damage manufactures.
unused_evidence: Locus B as a calibrator of the error split: the error process is shared by both loci, yet the error-model comparison (asymmetric vs symmetric 0.16 vs symmetric 0.01) is reported only for locus A. A joint fit with a shared split was not run.

sample_year: used only as a monotonicity check (about 37 years per generation). It marks the data as ancient and spans 2000 years; neither team asked whether a constant damage rate across that age range is plausible, though the constant seq_error column gives no handle to model otherwise.
Ne_schedule generations 0-5 (before the first sample at generation 6): whether and how this stretch enters the model (initial state) is not recorded by either team.
The symmetric-0.01 log-likelihood: team A ran it (s_A = 0.045) but recorded no fit statistic, so the three error readings are not ranked on a common footing.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams name the same weakest point: the 0.31/0.01 split is inferred and s_A moves from about 0.045 (symmetric 0.01) through 0.06 (symmetric 0.16) to 0.096 (asymmetric). Both only reported it. Neither estimated the split from the data (profile over e_CT with e_CT + e_TC = 0.32, both loci jointly) nor propagated its uncertainty into the interval for s.

Team A's second weak point: a piecewise-s improvement at generation 26 (s1 = 0.15, s2 = 0.05, LRT 5.3). It was tested only in the deterministic fit, not in the drift HMM, and only under the asymmetric error model, where the late points are at the error floor. It was set aside as post hoc; whether constant s 'fits adequately' was not shown by any goodness-of-fit test.

Team B recorded no pitfall checks at all (pitfalls_checked is empty): no constant-vs-piecewise s test, no deterministic-vs-drift comparison, and no statement of how the Ne schedule changed the estimate.
Team B tested sensitivity to T->C from 0.001 to 0.1 but did not record what s did across that range.
second_readings: 'Assume instrument-driven sequencing error is ~1%' together with 'seq_error is the average of the two directional miscall rates' has at least three readings: (i) use 1% symmetric and treat the 0.16 column as something else; (ii) use the column symmetrically at 0.16, as the library guidance said; (iii) 1% instrument error in both directions plus one-directional damage making up the average (the teams' reading). The three give s_A of roughly 0.045, 0.06 and 0.096, a factor of two, so the reported number rests on reading (iii).

'Selection coefficient s' for a haploid locus can be the Wrightian per-generation fitness advantage (w = 1 + s) or the logit-slope / Malthusian rate. Team A states s = exp(slope) - 1; team B does not say which its HMM uses. The gap is small at this s (about 5% relative) but should be stated.
'Estimate s' with a constant value: if selection decelerates, 'the' s could mean the early-phase value or the series average; team A's own piecewise fit gives 0.15 early and 0.05 late.
The locus choice (A) does not depend on any of these readings; only the magnitude of s does.
challenge.verdict: I trust the locus choice (A) and the sign of s: they hold under every error model either team tried. I do not yet trust the magnitude: s_A ranges from about 0.045 to 0.096 depending on an error split that both teams inferred with the same argument, and that argument's key premise (36/40 'impossible' under symmetric 0.16) is a roughly 1-in-5 sampling event, so the agreement between teams reflects a shared assumption rather than independent confirmation.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your case against the symmetric 0.16 error model rests on locus A gen 6 (36/40 = 0.90 > 0.84) being 'impossible', but for 40 reads at a true rate of 0.84 the chance of 36 or more is about 0.21. Refit all three error models (asymmetric 0.31/0.01, symmetric 0.16, symmetric 0.01) with identical HMM settings and report the log-likelihood for locus A, for locus B, for both jointly, and for locus A with the gen-6 sample left out. Does the preference for the asymmetric model survive at locus B and without that one sample, and does the result change your method or the uncertainty you attach to s?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You name the 0.31/0.01 split as your weakest point but only report it. Profile the likelihood over the split itself (C->T rate free, T->C = 0.32 minus it, shared by both loci, s and starting frequency re-optimised at each value) and report the likelihood-supported range of the split and the s_A estimate at each end of that range. Locus A's late T fractions (0.33-0.45) sit at the assumed 0.31 floor, so state how far s_A moves when the floor moves within its supported range. Does this change your point estimate or widen your interval?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your piecewise-s test (break at generation 26, s 0.15 then 0.05, LRT 5.3) was run in the deterministic fit and only under the asymmetric error model. Repeat it inside the drift HMM with the Ne schedule, under each error model, and add a goodness-of-fit test of the constant-s model (for example simulating trajectories and read counts from the fitted model and comparing a fit statistic). Is the deceleration still present with drift modelled, and does it appear only under the error model that puts the late samples on the error floor? Does the result change whether constant s is adequate and which interval defines the s you report?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your notes do not say how the hidden chain starts or how N enters. Report s_A and its interval under (a) the chain started at generation 0 versus at generation 6, (b) a flat prior on starting frequency versus a starting frequency estimated as a free parameter, and (c) drift variance p(1-p)/N versus p(1-p)/(2N) and N halved. Does any of these move s_A by more than a small fraction of its confidence interval, and if so does it change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your case against the symmetric 0.16 error model rests on locus A gen 6 (36/40 = 0.90 > 0.84) being 'impossible', but for 40 reads at a true rate of 0.84 the chance of 36 or more is about 0.21. Refit the asymmetric 0.31/0.01, symmetric 0.16 and symmetric 0.01 models with identical HMM settings and report the log-likelihood for locus A, for locus B, for both jointly, and for locus A with the gen-6 sample left out. Does the preference for the asymmetric model survive at locus B and without that one sample, and does the result change your method or the uncertainty you attach to s?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You tested T->C rates from 0.001 to 0.1 but did not record what s did, and your interval for s (0.04-0.165) holds the split fixed. Profile the likelihood over the split (C->T free, T->C = 0.32 minus it, shared by both loci, other parameters re-optimised) and report the supported range of the split and s_A at each end. Locus A's late T fractions (0.33-0.45) sit at the assumed 0.31 floor. Does the spread of s_A over the supported splits change your point estimate or your stated interval?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your record lists no pitfall checks and no test of constant selection. Inside your HMM, compare constant s with piecewise s at the Ne-schedule boundaries (generations 18/19, 26/27, 37/38) for locus A by likelihood ratio, correcting for the number of breakpoints tried, and compare the HMM estimate with a deterministic no-drift fit. Is there evidence that s differs between the early rise and the late samples near the error floor, and does it change whether a single s is the right quantity to report?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: State three modelling choices your notes leave open and report s_A under the alternative for each: (a) whether your HMM's s is the per-generation fitness advantage (w = 1 + s) or a logit slope, (b) whether the chain starts at generation 0 or generation 6 and with what prior on starting frequency, (c) whether drift variance uses N or 2N. Does any alternative move s_A by more than a small fraction of its interval, and does that change the method?

studies.title: Structural variant dosage and disease risk

shared_assumptions: Both teams put the outer-orientation dosage into the clinical outcome model as a covariate and reported the B coefficient from that joint model (-0.27) as the 'total-effect' odds ratio. Both saw that the B-only weighted estimate is about half the size (team-a: -0.13), but neither argued from the data whether the outer orientation is a confounder of B (to be adjusted) or part of the structure on which segment-B copies sit (so that conditioning on it turns a total effect into a partial one). 'Separating B from outer' can be satisfied in the calibration step alone.

Both teams assumed that reliability of a long-read call is unrelated to the segment-B copy number itself (reliable 483 samples = a representative training set). local_complexity is described as repeat complexity around the breakpoint, which could depend on genotype; neither team tested whether QC failure depends on B dosage, case status or ancestry.

Both teams assumed a single pooled marker-to-B calibration (ridge on all 60 markers) transports to all ancestries and from panel to non-panel cohort members, and that one pooled B log OR describes the source population, although team-a found per-ancestry estimates of opposite sign (EUR +0.31, EAS -1.06).

Both teams took the inverse-sample_fraction weights at face value. Fractions range from 0.002 to 0.84, so a few control rows carry weights in the hundreds; the sign of the estimate flips between unweighted (+0.11) and weighted (-0.27) fits, yet neither team showed how many observations the weighted estimate effectively rests on.

Both teams treated the expression slope as a sample-level quantity (unweighted OLS in the 560-sample expression panel, team-b without case status) although the task sentence attaches 'full-cohort source-population' to both the clinical association and the expression support, and how the expression panel was selected was not examined.
Both teams chose GENE2 over GENE1 on the multimapping argument alone, assuming a gene with multimapping reads cannot be the truly supported gene.
unused_evidence: marker_info.tsv.gz: mean_impute_info (0.905 for M007-M015, 0.925 for M025-M036, 0.985 elsewhere) and position_kb were not used by either team. The low-information blocks sit inside interval_1 and interval_2, the intervals team-a found to tag outer and B respectively, so they probably mark the structural segments; whether the calibration leans on these lower-quality markers, and whether their quality differs between panel and non-panel samples or by ancestry, was not checked.

breakpoint_panel depth_log2_segment_B: an independent depth-based read-out of segment-B copies that exists for all 780 panel samples, including the 297 QC failures. Team-b used it only to validate rounding in clean samples; team-a's record does not mention it. It is the one field that could show whether QC-failed samples differ in B dosage from reliable ones.
expression_panel membership itself (560 of 1900, 42% overlap with the breakpoint panel) and its relation to case, ancestry, tissue_source and design stratum was not analysed as a selection step.
GENE3 is not discussed in either record beyond the implicit statement that it has no signal.
unresolved_weak_points: Team-a named the ancestry heterogeneity of the B log OR (EUR +0.31, AFR -0.31, EAS -1.06) as its weakest point and kept the pooled estimate without finding out whether the heterogeneity comes from ancestry-specific tagging, from the weights, or from the outer adjustment. Reported, not resolved. Team-b did not report per-ancestry estimates at all.

Both teams named the imprecision and weight-dependence of the clinical log OR (SE 0.19-0.20, CI crosses 0), on which the sign and therefore target_support_code depend. Team-b bootstrapped but did not propagate calibration uncertainty. Reported, not resolved.

Team-a noted that GENE1 keeps a residual B effect after technical adjustment (0.44, B x multimapper interaction 0.39) so the choice of GENE2 rests on the multimapping profile only. Reported, not resolved.

Team-b said its QC thresholds were chosen by eye. This one is partly resolved by agreement: team-a's different thresholds give the same 483 reliable samples and 195 carriers, but neither team reported how many reliable samples sit near the rounding boundary.
second_readings: 'Total-effect odds ratio ... per additional calibrated segment-B copy': may mean the B effect without conditioning on the outer orientation (and certainly without conditioning on post-outcome design variables), with 'separating' done at the calibration stage; or the B effect conditional on outer dosage, as both teams reported. The two readings give about -0.13 versus -0.27.

'Full-cohort source-population ... molecular expression support': may require the expression slope to be weighted to the source population (team-a's own weighted value 0.286) rather than an unweighted, case-adjusted panel slope (0.308 / 0.321).

'Calibrated segment-B copy': may mean the long-read copy index after calibration to integer copies (both teams' reading), or a copy index that must first be put on a per-copy scale using the depth read-out before rounding; this matters only if cluster centres of copy_index_segment_B are not at integers.
'The expression-supported gene' presumes exactly one gene; if GENE1's slope at a normal multimapper fraction equals GENE2's, the data do not single one out and the choice needs an explicit rule.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust in n_calibrated_carriers (195, reached with two different threshold sets) and in the choice and rough size of the GENE2 slope; low trust in subhap_log_or and hence target_support_code, because its sign flips with the weights, differs across ancestry groups, has an interval that crosses zero, and its size roughly halves under the other reasonable reading of 'total effect' (no outer adjustment). The agreement reflects a shared recipe from the same library guidance, not independent confirmation.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you named the per-ancestry heterogeneity of the B log OR (EUR +0.31, AFR -0.31, EAS -1.06) as your weakest point but only reported it. Refit the marker-to-B calibration separately within each ancestry group (or with ancestry-by-marker terms), compare those predicted dosages with your pooled ones, and then test the B-by-ancestry interaction formally in the weighted model, also once unweighted and once without the outer term. Does the heterogeneity come from tagging, from the weights, or from the outer adjustment, and does the result change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the task asks for a 'total-effect' odds ratio, and your weighted B estimate is -0.13 without the outer-orientation term and -0.27 with it. In the reliable panel, tabulate integer B copies against integer outer dosage and report the outer coefficient with its interval from the joint model, then state from that evidence whether outer orientation acts as a separate confounder of B or as the background on which B copies sit, and therefore which of the two models estimates a total effect of B. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the sign of your B log OR flips between the unweighted and the weighted fit, and the weights span roughly 1.2 to several hundred. Compute the effective sample size of the weighted fit, the share of total weight carried by the ten heaviest rows, and the B estimate when those rows are removed one at a time and when weights are capped or stabilised. Does the weighted sign rest on a handful of heavily weighted controls, and does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: your choice of GENE2 rests on GENE1's multimapping profile, yet GENE1 keeps a B slope of 0.44 with a B-by-multimapper interaction of 0.39. Evaluate the GENE1 slope at the multimapper fraction typical of the other genes (and in your low-multimapper subset) and compare it with the GENE2 slope; separately, test a B-by-case interaction for GENE2 to see whether your sample-level slope (0.308) and your source-population-weighted slope (0.286) differ for a real reason, given that the task attaches 'full-cohort source-population' to the expression support too. Does either result change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the task asks for a 'total-effect' odds ratio, and you fitted B jointly with the outer-orientation dosage; you also found 26 B carriers with outer dosage 0. Report the weighted B estimate with and without the outer term side by side, the outer coefficient with its interval, and the B-by-outer table in the reliable panel, then state from that evidence whether conditioning on outer dosage gives a total effect of B or a partial one. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: your record gives one pooled B log OR and adjusts for PCs but not ancestry_group, and it shows calibration accuracy by ancestry but no clinical estimate by ancestry. Fit the weighted model within each ancestry group and test the B-by-ancestry interaction, and repeat with the calibration fitted within ancestry. Is the pooled sign shared by the groups, and do the weights (with the effective sample size and the share of weight on the ten heaviest rows) or the tagging drive any difference? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: your calibration assumes the 483 reliable samples are representative of the panel, but local_complexity describes repeats around the breakpoint and could depend on the genotype itself. Using depth_log2_segment_B, which exists for all 780 samples, compare the depth-based copy distribution (and case status and ancestry) between reliable and QC-failed samples, and among the 483 count how many copy_index values lie within 0.2 of a rounding boundary and whether depth agrees with the rounded call there. Does QC failure depend on segment-B dosage, and does that change the calibration or the carrier count?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: your expression model has no case-status term and no sampling weights, although the expression panel is a subset of a cohort that is 81% cases and the task attaches 'full-cohort source-population' to the expression support. Check whether log_expr of GENE2 differs by case status, whether expression-panel membership depends on case, ancestry or design stratum, and how the GENE2 slope moves when case is added, when a B-by-case term is added, and when inverse sample_fraction weights are used; also give the GENE1 slope at a multimapper fraction typical of the other genes. Does any of this change your method or your choice of gene?

questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team applied barcode-level QC, fixed before looking at genotype, that flagged total-UMI outliers and droplets whose HBB is far in excess of what ambient contamination could explain (red-blood-cell-contaminated droplets), and estimated contamination only after setting those aside. Your notes record duplicate checks but no barcode QC, and your contamination model assumes all HBB in a cell is ambient. Check whether such barcodes exist in your data, how many there are per donor and per genotype, and whether your per-donor contamination estimates move when they are set aside. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the activated state from the ISG markers only after removing the ambient contribution to those markers, on the grounds that the ambient profile itself contains ISG transcripts and contamination differs between donors. Your clustering used an ISG/LST1 score with no recorded ambient adjustment, and the two teams ended with different numbers of activated cells. Check whether the cluster assignment of any cells, especially in the high-contamination donors, changes when the ambient contribution to the gating markers is accounted for, and which donors those cells belong to. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the way the ambient expectation is removed (per cell with clipping at zero, per donor without clipping, or as a term in the model mean) changes the estimate, and that ambient makes up the majority of activated-cell CXCL10 counts in the most contaminated donors. Check in your mixture-mean fit what share of each donor's expected CXCL10 count is the ambient term, how much information the most contaminated donors actually contribute to the genotype coefficient, and whether the coefficient is stable to the dispersion and to how those donors are weighted. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team counted activated cells per donor and applied (and varied) a minimum number of activated cells for a donor to enter the pseudobulk fit, because the activated fraction is small in some genotype groups. Your notes do not record such a check. Tabulate activated cells per donor in your data and check whether any donor enters your fit on very few cells. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team estimated a separate contamination fraction for each donor, whereas your notes describe contamination as two donor groups and your plan mentioned a per-cell estimate. State at which level (cell, donor, donor group) the contamination fraction in your final model is estimated, how precisely HBB counts pin it down at that level, and whether the genotype coefficient moves when the level is changed. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team did not take the HBB-derived contamination scale on trust: they let a multiplier on the ambient CXCL10 term be estimated from the data, once in activated cells only and once jointly with the resting cells, and found the genotype coefficient very sensitive to that multiplier. Your notes record no test of the ambient scale. Check in your data what multiplier the counts themselves support, in the activated stratum alone and when the resting stratum is included, and how your coefficient responds across a plausible range. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team fitted the same ambient-corrected model in the resting cluster and used it as a check on whether the ambient correction is complete. Check what your corrected CXCL10 rates look like in the resting stratum across donors and contamination levels, and whether that pattern is what you would expect if the ambient removal were right. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the activated state from ISG and LST1 jointly and obtained a different number of activated cells from you. You recorded that ISG-high and LST1-low agree for most but not all cells. Check the cells where your ISG gate and LST1 status disagree: which donors and genotypes they come from, what their CXCL10 and contamination look like, and whether your estimate moves when they are assigned the other way. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team estimated the endogenous rate and the ambient term together in one donor-level negative-binomial mean model, rather than subtracting first and fitting afterwards. You recorded strong overdispersion between donors, yet your ambient-in-mean version was a Poisson fit, and your headline figure combines it with a subtract-then-fit version. Check how donors whose corrected count is near or below zero are handled in each version, whether the two versions weight the heavily contaminated donors the same way, and which single version you judge correct and why. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team ran leave-one-donor-out and a donor bootstrap, and described contamination as falling into two donor groups rather than varying donor by donor. Your notes record neither a leave-one-out check nor how precisely each donor's rho is determined. Check whether any single donor drives your coefficient, how noisy the donor-specific rho values are given the HBB counts behind them, and whether the coefficient moves if rho is shared within the two contamination groups. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team checked the input for duplicate barcode IDs and duplicate rows before analysis, and did not remove cells by UMI or HBB thresholds. Your notes record cell QC but no duplicate check. Check whether duplicates exist in your data, and report how many cells per donor and genotype your QC removed and whether removal is balanced across the contamination groups. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both use the same pipeline (HBB-based donor contamination rho, ISG gate, donor-pseudobulk NB with an additive ambient term). They differ only in the ambient scale k: X fixes k=1 (the empty-drop profile times the HBB-derived rho), giving -0.34. Y estimates k from the data (1.27, using the resting stratum and the split g=1 donors), giving -0.54.
referee.test: Within genotype g=1 (genotype held fixed: 4 high-rho and 4 low-rho donors), I computed the ambient-corrected rate (y - k*rho*N*amb)/(N*(1-rho)) for high-rho and low-rho donors and solved for the k that makes the two groups equal. I did this for genes Y did not use to set k (resting IFI6 and ISG15, which are mostly ambient in resting cells) as well as for CXCL10, with a 2000-rep donor bootstrap. Code: test.py.
referee.reason: An independent gene (ISG15) and resting CXCL10 both reject k=1 and point to a k above 1, close to Y's 1.27. So X's fixed scale leaves ambient CXCL10 in the high-contamination donors, which are mostly higher-genotype donors, and that biases beta upward toward 0. The size of the effect is still uncertain: k from about 1.15 to 1.6 maps to beta from about -0.45 to -0.75. Y's -0.54 sits inside that range, so I give no own answer.

questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that cohort_roster rows are not all of one kind: they differ in family_history_tier, and the screen-positive rate is not the same across tiers within each ancestry. Your checks list a tier breakdown of screening carrier rates, but your record does not say which rows went into carrier_frequency_afr and carrier_frequency_eur. Tabulate cohort_roster by collection x ancestry x family_history_tier (and any field that marks adults), check whether the tiers differ in your data, and state which rows you judge the task to mean by 'screening-roster adults' and why. Does it change your method, including the prior that goes into the AFR screen-negative residual risk?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team treated the partner term row by row: a tested partner row carries its own assay result (read with lot_C42 calibration), and an untested row carries a prior that does not come from the tested partners. You recorded that 280 of 500 partner rows sit in one site x wave x family-history stratum where only 14 were tested, and that your figure rests on missing-at-random within strata. Check (a) how much of your full-roster estimate comes from those 14 rows, (b) whether the tested rows in that stratum look like a random draw from it on every roster field you have (ancestry, tier, any reason-for-testing field), and (c) whether the carrier rates you infer for tested partners are compatible with the screening-roster rates for the same ancestry and family-history tier after allowing for the different reagent lot. Does it change your method for the untested rows?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that DRX1_T02 deletion sensitivity in the controls differs between the two reagent lots within the same ancestry, as well as between ancestries, and that some deletion-like calls in 'none' controls survive the segmental-duplication filter and cannot be told apart from true deletions. Your recorded AFR deletion sensitivity pools controls from both lots. Check whether deletion sensitivity and the remaining false-positive rate differ by lot within ancestry in your data, and whether the AFR detection rate behind your residual risk uses only the lot the screening roster was run on. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that in partner_roster the positive-call rate among tested partners differs a lot between intake_site x collection_wave strata, and that testing completion also depends on site x wave x family-history tier (one site is fully tested, while the largest stratum has very few tested rows). Your partner strata use ancestry x tier and testing result only. Tabulate partner_roster by intake_site x collection_wave x family_history_tier x testing_status, check whether this holds in your data, and check whether a prior for untested partners taken from the screening cohort by ancestry x tier agrees with the tested partners in the same site x wave stratum. Does it change your method for the untested rows?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the two teams did not use the same cohort_roster rows for the carrier frequencies. You excluded the family_history_tier 1 rows although every cohort row has collection = screening; the other team did not record such an exclusion. Check whether the roster or the task text gives any basis, other than the difference in positive rate, for saying tier-1 rows are not 'screening-roster adults' (for example a field for ascertainment route, referral, or age), and state which reading of the estimand you judge the task to mean and why. Check also whether the AFR screen-negative residual risk should use the same row set as carrier_frequency_afr. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found allele dropout at DRX1_T01 in class_01 controls (VAF near zero in true carriers) at a rate that differs between AFR and EUR, and corrected class proportions jointly with an ancestry x batch misclassification matrix instead of one class at a time. Check in your controls whether class_01 sensitivity differs by ancestry as well as by lot, whether your het window (VAF 0.3-0.7, depth >= 20) loses true carriers beyond the dropout cases, and whether any control of one class is called as another class or as two classes, which a per-class correction would not account for. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both teams use effectively the same per-person calling rules: in this data the VAF windows 0.3-0.7 and >=0.2 give identical calls, and segdup 0.55 vs 0.6 also gives identical calls. Both include all 800 screening rows, and both treat partners as MAR within site x wave strata. The screening carrier frequencies differ because of the misclassification correction. X used per-class Rogan-Gladen (AFR 0.0986, EUR 0.0767). Y reports a joint EM over ancestry x lot confusion matrices (AFR 0.0926, EUR 0.0703). The partner term differs because of the stratum model: X scales the cohort prior per site x wave (0.210), and Y uses shrunk site x wave x tier EM (0.2215).
referee.test: test.py, calls.py and t2.py rebuild the calls and the lot_A17 per-ancestry 4x4 confusion matrix from the controls. They then (a) recompute both corrections, (b) fit the exact joint EM/MLE that Y describes, and (c) compute profile-likelihood LRs for the screening call counts at X's and Y's carrier frequencies. For partners they compute unshrunk stratified EM on lot_C42 under three stratifications.
referee.reason: X's screening estimates can be reproduced exactly and sit close to the joint MLE. Y's stated method, run on the same matrices, gives values on the opposite side of X, so Y's reported numbers do not follow from its own method. The partner term cannot be separated by the data (sampling and model uncertainty are large), and the difference there is small (about 5%). The exact joint MLE is slightly better than RG, because carriers of the other classes show no deletion false positives in the controls. It is given as own_answer, using X's partner term.

studies.title: CRISPRi screen of long non-coding RNAs

questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that a few of the non-targeting control guides, and a few of the ANKRD42 control guides, have screen log fold changes far from the rest of the controls, consistently across replicates. Your record says you centred on the non-targeting controls but does not say you looked at them one by one. Check the per-guide log fold change of every control guide in your data, and how your matched-control centre is affected by any that stand apart. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found several targeting guides whose measured local knockdown is strong but whose screen growth looks like that of the controls, again with good replicate agreement. Your joint CRISPRi regression kept all locus guides in an ordinary least-squares fit. Check whether such guides exist in your data, which gene's knockdown they carry, and how much leverage they have on each coefficient of your joint fit. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that guide GC fraction is associated with the screen log fold change among control guides that have no local knockdown, and that GC fraction is not balanced across the locus guides (the distal LINC473-only guides differ in GC from the proximal LINC473 and KIN1 guides). You recorded the high-GC pitfall as not found. Check, among the control guides only, whether log fold change depends on guide_gc_frac, and whether GC is aligned with the knockdown pattern in the locus guides. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you noted that the low-overlap CasRx guides all sit on plate C. The other team found that plate is fully confounded with isoform-overlap class in the CasRx file, and that the plates in the single-guide follow-up file carry offsets that can be measured against the pooled screen. Check whether the plates of your retained high-overlap CasRx guides differ from one another, whether the follow-up file shows plate-level offsets relative to the screen, and whether your extrapolation is the same within each plate. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team observed that in the low-overlap CasRx guides growth still scales with knockdown_efficiency, although those guides barely touch the dominant isoform. You excluded those guides as collateral or off-target. Check whether whatever produces that growth in the low-overlap guides could also be present in the high-overlap guides you kept, that is, whether part of the slope of growth on knockdown_efficiency among your retained guides could be something other than dominant-transcript loss. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the task defines lncrna_specific_lfc as a pooled-screen matched-control day-10 effect, but your estimate is read directly from the CasRx growth_lfc values. The other team checked whether follow-up growth measurements are on the same scale as the pooled screen by comparing the single-guide follow-up file with the screen for the guides present in both. Check in your data whether follow-up growth and screen log fold change agree one-to-one for shared guides, and whether the CasRx assay shares that scale. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team did not model the low-overlap CasRx guides at all; it set them aside as collateral or off-target and estimated the transcript effect only from guides with major_isoform_overlap of at least 0.5. Your dominant-isoform coefficient is fitted jointly with a non-dominant term driven mainly by the plate C guides. Check what your dominant-isoform estimate is when it is fitted on the high-overlap guides alone (with your plate calibration), and whether the low-overlap guides are pulling the dominant-isoform coefficient through the shared intercept or plate terms. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you kept a nonzero CasRx intercept as a nonspecific term and recorded that your estimate depends on that choice. The other team compared free-intercept and through-origin fits and also checked, in the pooled CRISPRi regression, whether zero knockdown corresponds to zero growth effect. Check what independent evidence in your data (for example CasRx guides with little or no knockdown, or control wells on the same plates) supports a nonspecific CasRx offset separate from the plate offsets you already fixed, and whether the intercept and the plate offsets are separately identified. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team treated knockdown_efficiency and the local expr_rel values as single noisy measurements per guide and compared ordinary least squares with an errors-in-variables fit, because noise in the knockdown measurement attenuates a slope that is then extrapolated to 100% knockdown. Your record shows no such check. Check the spread and range of the knockdown values in the CasRx and local-expression tables and whether measurement error in knockdown is large enough to matter for either of your extrapolated coefficients. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team kept every locus guide in its joint CRISPRi regression, whereas you removed ten guides, five of them targeting guides with strong measured knockdown and control-like growth. Check which gene's knockdown (LINC473, KIN1 or both) those five guides carry, whether the rule that removed them was independent of how well they fit the knockdown model, and how each coefficient behaves with all guides kept under your robust fit. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you used the single-guide follow-up file to calibrate plate offsets and a slope against the screen, and then applied those offsets to the CasRx plates. The other team used the same file differently, as an independent check of how growth tracks KIN1 and LINC473 knockdown across the follow-up guides. Check whether the follow-up plates and the CasRx plates are demonstrably the same physical plates or batches (and not only plates with the same labels), whether plate in the follow-up file is itself confounded with which gene the guides repress, and whether the follow-up growth-versus-knockdown relation agrees with your screen coefficients. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team looked for a high-GC or off-target signal among the CRISPRi guides and recorded that it did not find one, while you fitted a GC covariate from the non-targeting and ANKRD42 guides. Check how many control guides the GC term rests on once your outlier guides are removed, whether the GC dependence is distinguishable from zero given their scatter, and how each locus coefficient behaves with and without the GC term. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both agree neighbor_mediated_lfc ~ -0.73/-0.75 and advance_target=0. They differ on lncrna_specific_lfc: X fits CasRx growth = int + b_dom*kd*overlap + b_non*kd*(1-overlap) pooled across plates with no plate term, giving int+b_dom = -0.17; Y adds plate offsets (calibrated from guide_followup) and excludes the intercept, giving b_dom = -0.05. Plate is confounded with overlap (plate A = high-overlap guides).
referee.test: test.py: (1) fit the CasRx dominant/non-dominant decomposition separately within each plate, where plate cannot be confounded with overlap; (2) estimate plate offsets internally from CasRx (plate fixed effects) and independently from guide_followup vs pooled-screen LFC, and compare.
referee.reason: The dominant-transcript effect is ~-0.05 consistently within every plate, and independent follow-up data confirm the plate batch offsets that X's model ignores. So lncrna_specific_lfc ~ -0.05 (> -0.08). Neighbor effect ~ -0.75 is agreed by both, and advance_target=0 under either answer.

questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the disease marginal z-scores fall off with distance from a peak faster than the EUR correlation reference predicts, while the phase-2 protein z-scores follow the reference. Your LD checks are recorded as finding no problem, but they do not say whether they were run on the disease file separately from the protein files. Check, for the disease statistics alone and for each protein alone, how the z-scores of the neighbours of a strong peak (for example the disease-only peak rs200068, and a protein lead SNP) compare with what the reference predicts at lag 1, 2 and 3. Does the reference describe the disease data as well as it describes the protein data, and does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team recorded that two of the disease-only peaks lie right next to protein lead SNPs (rs200028 beside rs200024/rs200025, and rs200050 beside rs200047). Your rule removes every SNP with r2>=0.05 to those peaks. List which SNPs the rule removes, and check whether the strongest and the conditionally independent lead SNPs for PROTA and for PROTB are among them. Among the 47 SNPs you keep, which signals actually identify each protein's effect, and are those SNPs independent signals or only the LD tails of removed leads? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team kept the SNPs near the disease-only peaks and modelled those variants as explicit effects, and it attributes much of the heterogeneity to the correlation reference not fitting the disease data. You rejected stepwise modelling because it did not converge, and your exclusion set and LD threshold were chosen from the data until Q matched its degrees of freedom. Check whether the failure of your stepwise fit to converge is related to how well the reference fits the disease statistics, and whether a Q close to its degrees of freedom on the retained SNPs could arise from having removed the informative region rather than from a correct model. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team did not model the disease-only variants; it removed all SNPs in LD with three disease-only peaks (rs200028, rs200050, rs200068) and then found residual heterogeneity consistent with its degrees of freedom using the EUR reference unchanged. Your models keep a residual Q several times its degrees of freedom under every LD model you tried. Check whether, on the SNPs that are not in LD with those three peaks, the disease statistics are consistent with the EUR reference and with your protein model, and whether the misfit you see is confined to the neighbourhoods of the disease-only peaks or is present across the locus. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team identified three protein-independent disease peaks, whereas you modelled 9 to 12 disease-only variants and replaced the reference with a one-parameter AR(rho) correlation for the disease data. Check whether each of your additional modelled variants is a distinct signal or appears only because of the assumed disease LD model, whether any of them is in LD with a protein lead SNP so that it could absorb protein-mediated signal, and whether the observed pairwise structure of the disease z-scores supports a single AR(rho) form. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team computed LD-aware conditional F statistics for each protein on its final instrument set, found one protein borderline weak conditional on the other, and used weights that include the uncertainty of the phase-2 protein betas. Your plan lists a conditional F check, but none is recorded for your final models built on 6 conditionally independent leads. Compute the conditional instrument strength for each protein in your final models and check whether the standard errors of the phase-2 betas enter your weights. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team submitted the estimate of one fitted specification that it could defend with a heterogeneity test. Your submitted values are a central value taken across several specifications, each of which you describe as fitting poorly. Check whether any single specification of yours can be justified from the data on its own fit, and whether the spread across your specifications is driven by one modelling choice (the disease LD parameter, the set of modelled disease-only variants, or the instrument set). Does it change your method?

questions.q: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team compared, marker by marker, the RIL calls with the allele of the founder haplotype inferred from the neighbouring markers, and found that two chromosome 1 markers lying close to the peak region disagree far more often than any other marker, with the founders.tsv alleles at those two markers looking opposite to the RIL alleles for all 8 founders. Your records show no per-marker check of founder-versus-RIL agreement. Check whether that holds in your data: compute the per-marker mismatch between RIL calls and your inferred haplotypes (leaving the tested marker out), and see whether any markers near the peak stand out and whether your founder haplotype probabilities and founder effects at the peak change depending on how those markers are treated. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the 8 founders are very unevenly represented at the chromosome 1 peak, that one of the nearly tied candidate founders is carried by about half the number of lines expected for an equal split and that its lines are unevenly spread over the two batches, and that the ranking of the tied founders depends on whether plain fixed-effect coefficients or shrunken (random-effect) estimates are used. Your records rank the founders by point estimates without per-founder line counts or standard errors. Check in your data: the expected number of lines per founder at the peak (sum of haplotype probabilities), the standard error of each founder effect, the batch split of each candidate founder's lines, and whether your ranking of the tied founders is the same under shrunken estimates. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you recorded that the founder you reported is not the founder that comes out on top most often in your own bootstrap, and that the three candidate founders have almost identical estimated effects. The other team's bootstrap and its point estimates pointed to one and the same founder for that team. Check why your two lines of evidence disagree: is the top founder in each bootstrap resample read at a re-estimated peak or at a fixed position, how sharply does your HMM assign each line to one founder at the peak (how many lines have a maximum founder probability above one half, and can the candidate founders be told apart from the local SNP pattern), and do the raw phenotype means of lines hard-called to each candidate founder, adjusted for batch, agree with your coefficients? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the chromosome 2 signal is not a localised peak: the 8-founder LOD stays elevated along the whole of chromosome 2 and its support interval spans the entire chromosome, which that team read as diffuse background rather than a single locus, and it therefore also controlled background with a mixed model using kinship computed from chromosome 2. You added the chromosome 2 peak as a single covariate and counted that model among those deciding the founder. Check whether that holds in your data: the shape of your chromosome 2 LOD curve, and whether the ranking of the tied founders at the chromosome 1 peak is the same with no chromosome 2 control, with the single covariate, and with a kinship-based control. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you reported a position that is the midpoint between the peaks of two different analyses (with and without the outlying line), so it is not the maximum of any single LOD curve. The other team reported the maximum of one stated primary model, scanned on a regular 1 cM pseudomarker grid, and quoted a support interval around it. Check which single model you judge to be the primary one for this task and why, where its LOD curve peaks on a regular grid, and whether the choice matters relative to the width of your support interval. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found a single line with an extreme phenotype value, far below every other line in its batch, and found that leaving that one line out moves the chromosome 1 peak position and changes the LOD by about one unit. Your records show a rank-based transform but no check of the influence of individual lines. Check whether that holds in your data: identify the most extreme phenotype value after batch adjustment, see which founder haplotype that line carries at the peak, and see whether the peak position, the LOD against your permutation threshold, and the ranking of the tied founders change when that line is left out. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team compared the nearly tied candidate founders with one-founder-versus-the-rest contrast models at the peak and with scans run separately within each batch. You recorded that the lines carrying your top founder are few and unevenly spread over the two batches, but no within-batch or one-founder-versus-rest comparison. Check in your data whether the ranking of the tied founders is the same within each batch taken separately, and whether a one-founder-versus-rest contrast at the peak ranks the candidate founders in the same order as your 8-founder coefficients. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team treated the chromosome 2 peak as a covariate in the models from which it read the founder effects, and found that its chromosome 1 LOD changes by about one unit when that covariate is added. You recorded that your top founder changes when the chromosome 2 covariate is combined with shrinkage, yet you kept the chromosome 2 covariate as a sensitivity check only. Check what in the data decides whether chromosome 2 control belongs in the primary model (for example how much residual variance it removes, and whether chromosome 2 haplotypes are correlated with the candidate founders' haplotypes at the chromosome 1 peak), and state which founder ranking you obtain under the model you judge to be best supported, and why the rule you were given for reporting a founder under shrunken estimates is or is not met. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team kept every marker in its haplotype reconstruction and varied the amount of recombination assumed by the HMM (map expansion), while you removed two chromosome 1 markers next to the peak and varied only the genotyping error rate. Check whether the two markers you removed could instead be kept with their founder alleles recoded, and whether the ranking of the tied founders and the peak position are the same under the three treatments (kept as given, removed, recoded) and under different assumed amounts of recombination in your transition model. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: Both teams find the same position (45 vs 46 cM, both inside the other's interval) and both flip m1_056/m1_058. They differ only on the high founder: X says F4 and Y says F5. X puts the chr2 QTL in the primary model and ranks founders by REML-BLUP shrunken effects. Under X's own fixed effects F5 is first, so X's F4 comes from shrinkage pulling the rare F5 (about 7 lines) down. Y uses batch only and ranks by the fixed haplotype effects at the peak.
referee.test: test.py: my own 8-state selfed-RIL HMM (flipped markers recoded, monomorphic markers dropped) at two settings, err 0.005/map x1 and err 0.02/map x3. At 45 and 46 cM I fitted founder-mean regressions with batch only and with batch plus chr2-peak haplotypes. For each fit I computed the direct F5-F4 contrast (estimate, SE, t) and a 300-replicate bootstrap P(F5>F4) at the fixed peak. I also compared batch-adjusted phenotype means of confidently hard-called (posterior >0.8) F4 and F5 carriers, which is model-free.
referee.reason: The data favour F5 under every unshrunken model, including X's own primary batch+chr2 model, in the bootstrap and in model-free carrier means. X's switch to F4 depends only on BLUP shrinkage of a rare founder, which is an estimator choice and not evidence that F4 carriers score higher. The direct contrast never favours F4. The F5 call is weak (F5 vs F4 not significant), but no test outcome supports X over Y. Position about 45-46 cM; Y's 46.0 is the batch-only peak.

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team applied barcode-level QC, fixed before looking at genotype, that flagged total-UMI outliers and droplets whose HBB is far in excess of what ambient contamination could explain (red-blood-cell-contaminated droplets), and estimated contamination only after setting those aside. Your notes record duplicate checks but no barcode QC, and your contamination model assumes all HBB in a cell is ambient. Check whether such barcodes exist in your data, how many there are per donor and per genotype, and whether your per-donor contamination estimates move when they are set aside. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the activated state from the ISG markers only after removing the ambient contribution to those markers, on the grounds that the ambient profile itself contains ISG transcripts and contamination differs between donors. Your clustering used an ISG/LST1 score with no recorded ambient adjustment, and the two teams ended with different numbers of activated cells. Check whether the cluster assignment of any cells, especially in the high-contamination donors, changes when the ambient contribution to the gating markers is accounted for, and which donors those cells belong to. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that the way the ambient expectation is removed (per cell with clipping at zero, per donor without clipping, or as a term in the model mean) changes the estimate, and that ambient makes up the majority of activated-cell CXCL10 counts in the most contaminated donors. Check in your mixture-mean fit what share of each donor's expected CXCL10 count is the ambient term, how much information the most contaminated donors actually contribute to the genotype coefficient, and whether the coefficient is stable to the dispersion and to how those donors are weighted. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team counted activated cells per donor and applied (and varied) a minimum number of activated cells for a donor to enter the pseudobulk fit, because the activated fraction is small in some genotype groups. Your notes do not record such a check. Tabulate activated cells per donor in your data and check whether any donor enters your fit on very few cells. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team estimated a separate contamination fraction for each donor, whereas your notes describe contamination as two donor groups and your plan mentioned a per-cell estimate. State at which level (cell, donor, donor group) the contamination fraction in your final model is estimated, how precisely HBB counts pin it down at that level, and whether the genotype coefficient moves when the level is changed. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team did not take the HBB-derived contamination scale on trust: they let a multiplier on the ambient CXCL10 term be estimated from the data, once in activated cells only and once jointly with the resting cells, and found the genotype coefficient very sensitive to that multiplier. Your notes record no test of the ambient scale. Check in your data what multiplier the counts themselves support, in the activated stratum alone and when the resting stratum is included, and how your coefficient responds across a plausible range. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team fitted the same ambient-corrected model in the resting cluster and used it as a check on whether the ambient correction is complete. Check what your corrected CXCL10 rates look like in the resting stratum across donors and contamination levels, and whether that pattern is what you would expect if the ambient removal were right. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the activated state from ISG and LST1 jointly and obtained a different number of activated cells from you. You recorded that ISG-high and LST1-low agree for most but not all cells. Check the cells where your ISG gate and LST1 status disagree: which donors and genotypes they come from, what their CXCL10 and contamination look like, and whether your estimate moves when they are assigned the other way. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team estimated the endogenous rate and the ambient term together in one donor-level negative-binomial mean model, rather than subtracting first and fitting afterwards. You recorded strong overdispersion between donors, yet your ambient-in-mean version was a Poisson fit, and your headline figure combines it with a subtract-then-fit version. Check how donors whose corrected count is near or below zero are handled in each version, whether the two versions weight the heavily contaminated donors the same way, and which single version you judge correct and why. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team ran leave-one-donor-out and a donor bootstrap, and described contamination as falling into two donor groups rather than varying donor by donor. Your notes record neither a leave-one-out check nor how precisely each donor's rho is determined. Check whether any single donor drives your coefficient, how noisy the donor-specific rho values are given the HBB counts behind them, and whether the coefficient moves if rho is shared within the two contamination groups. Does it change your method?

sl-test-v2-4be8ec20a2a5.label: Polarize alt vs derived via outgroup
sl-test-v2-4be8ec20a2a5.text: PITFALL: alt_reads count the ALT allele, but s is defined for the DERIVED allele; if the outgroup_allele equals the alt allele, the alt allele is ancestral and the sign of s (and possibly which locus is 'more strongly positively selected') flips. CHECK: in variant_info.tsv compare outgroup_allele to ref and alt for each locus; derived = the allele that does NOT match the outgroup. IF FOUND: model derived frequency = 1 - alt frequency for that locus before fitting, then compare loci on derived-allele s (a locus whose alt falls in frequency may be the one with strong positive selection on the derived allele). Outgroup polarisation by parsimony can itself be wrong (homoplasy), so note it as an assumption. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6028244/ ; https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msm108

sl-test-v2-e574ae5b091b.label: Sequencing error correction in likelihood
sl-test-v2-e574ae5b091b.text: PITFALL: sequencing error makes observed frequencies too high near 0 and too low near 1 (p_obs = p(1-e) + (1-p)e under symmetric error), which flattens the logit trajectory and biases s toward 0, mostly when the allele is rare or near fixation. CHECK: look for samples where alt_reads/total_reads is within a few multiples of seq_error (about 0.01) of 0 or 1. IF FOUND: put the error inside the binomial likelihood, alt_reads ~ Binomial(total_reads, p(1-e)+(1-p)e), using each row's seq_error (it is already the average of the two directional rates, so the symmetric form is appropriate). Do not plug raw frequencies or 0/1 values into logit; do not just subtract the error and clip. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4040993/ ; https://hal.inrae.fr/hal-02794461

sl-test-v2-93db7d378319.label: Use binomial likelihood not raw logit OLS
sl-test-v2-93db7d378319.text: PITFALL: estimating s by OLS of logit(raw frequency) on generation ignores binomial read-sampling noise (variance ~ p(1-p)/depth) and gives infinite or unstable values at frequencies of 0 or 1. Different total_reads per sample also make equal weighting wrong. CHECK: inspect total_reads per sample and whether any frequency is at or near 0 or 1. IF FOUND: fit by maximum likelihood with a binomial (plus error) observation model at the read level, or at least use weighted least squares with weights depth*p(1-p). Report a CI from profile likelihood or bootstrap, not just a point estimate. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5850601/ ; https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.107.085019

sl-test-v2-04d31d8e8271.label: Use the Ne schedule: drift vs selection
sl-test-v2-04d31d8e8271.text: PITFALL: a provided Ne schedule (piecewise N by generation, e.g. a bottleneck) means drift variance differs between intervals. Ignoring it treats drift-driven jumps during low-N intervals as selection signal, and can mistake drift for selection when comparing two loci. CHECK: read Ne_schedule.tsv (gen_start, gen_end, N), see which sampling intervals fall in low-N periods, and see whether big frequency jumps line up with them. IF FOUND: use a Wright-Fisher HMM or diffusion model with time-varying N (e.g. a Mathieson-McVean-style HMM, Beta-with-spikes, or a Gaussian/Kalman approximation with drift variance p(1-p)/N per generation in each interval), so that drift and sampling noise are modelled separately from selection. Compare the result with the deterministic fit as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5062326/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6893182/

sl-test-v2-6a2044439889.label: Time units: generations not years
sl-test-v2-6a2044439889.text: PITFALL: the time series has both a 'generation' and a 'sample_year' column; fitting against years, or mixing them up, rescales s by the generations-per-year factor. s is defined per generation. CHECK: confirm that generation increases steadily, see how it relates to sample_year, and check that the Ne_schedule uses generation coordinates. IF FOUND: always use generation as the time axis for s and for Ne intervals; use sample_year only for QC (e.g. duplicate or out-of-order samples). SOURCE: https://github.com/steinrue/EMSel (years_to_gen option) ; https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsbl/article/7/2/210/48870/On-measuring-selection-in-experimental

sl-test-v2-9c5a0dd5bccb.label: Haploid model: slope=ln(1+s)
sl-test-v2-9c5a0dd5bccb.text: PITFALL: wrong selection model for haploids. For a haploid locus with relative fitness 1+s, p' = p(1+s)/(1+sp), so logit(p_t) = logit(p_0) + t*ln(1+s) exactly. A slope of the logit is ln(1+s), not s, and using diploid additive or dominance formulas is wrong. CHECK: decide whether the reported s is the slope r = ln(1+s) or s = exp(r) - 1, which differ noticeably when s > ~0.1. IF FOUND: fit the haploid recursion directly with s as the parameter, or convert the slope with s = exp(slope) - 1, and state the convention in the reasoning. SOURCE: https://www.icts.res.in/sites/default/files/popgen2016-Nick-Barton-2-2016-01-26_0.pdf ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5850601/

sl-test-v2-c85b1bacd1ee.label: Check constant-s assumption / saturation
sl-test-v2-c85b1bacd1ee.text: PITFALL: selection may not be constant over the whole series (e.g. it changes with environment or Ne epoch), or the allele may plateau or fix; a single-s fit then averages across regimes or is dominated by saturated points that carry little information. CHECK: plot error-corrected logit(derived freq) against generation for each locus, look for curvature or breakpoints (especially at Ne_schedule boundaries) and for samples stuck near 0 or 1, and compare a constant-s model with a piecewise-s model by likelihood ratio or AIC. IF FOUND: report the constant-s estimate only if it fits adequately; otherwise say so and justify which interval defines s. Points near fixation should carry little weight, which a correct binomial-plus-error likelihood does automatically. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.11.17.387761 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13223747/

sl-test-v2-64129d888d6c.label: Choose locus by formal comparison
sl-test-v2-64129d888d6c.text: PITFALL: picking the 'more strongly selected' locus by eye or by the larger raw frequency change can be wrong: drift in a small-Ne population, low depth, or polarisation can make the weaker locus look stronger. CHECK: estimate s for the derived allele at BOTH loci with the same model and give the uncertainty (CI) for each; check whether the CIs overlap and whether each locus differs from neutrality (LRT against s=0, accounting for drift under the Ne schedule). IF FOUND: base the locus choice on the derived-allele s estimates with CIs, and report both estimates in the reasoning. SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.0452v1.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.107.085019

sl-test-v2-aa84f551abb5.label: bias correction before O/E
sl-test-v2-aa84f551abb5.text: PITFALL: Raw counts carry per-bin visibility biases (GC content, mappability, restriction-site density are given in bins_20kb.tsv.gz), so O/E on raw counts can reflect anchor-bin bias rather than looping. CHECK: per replicate, correlate bin coverage (row sums) with gc_content, mappability and re_sites, and look at the row sums for bins 8 and 17 against the others. IF FOUND: balance each replicate's matrix (ICE/Sinkhorn, cis-only, excluding the first 1-2 diagonals) or fit an explicit Poisson/NB model with log(gc), log(mappability), log(re_sites) offsets before computing O/E. Report raw and corrected values. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3816492/ ; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.2144/btn-2019-0105

sl-test-v2-c4340eded099.label: distance-matched expected
sl-test-v2-c4340eded099.text: PITFALL: The expected value must be distance-matched. Using a global mean, or the wrong distance, makes the O/E meaningless. CHECK: confirm that the 8-17 pixel is on diagonal dist_bin = 9 (check that the dist_bin column equals bin_j - bin_i) and that the expected is the mean of all valid pixels on that same diagonal, in the same replicate, after the same normalization. IF FOUND: recompute expected per replicate per diagonal (cooltools expected_cis convention); never pool diagonals or use a whole-matrix mean. SOURCE: https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/contacts_vs_distance.html

sl-test-v2-8ec3904ebb1c.label: small-matrix expected noise
sl-test-v2-8ec3904ebb1c.text: PITFALL: The matrix covers only 24 bins at 20 kb, so diagonal 9 has only about 15 pixels. The expected there is noisy, can be pulled up by the loop pixel itself and by other loops or domain structure, and edge bins/bad bins skew it. CHECK: count the valid pixels on diagonal 9 and compare the mean with the median, with and without the 8-17 pixel. Also compare against a smoothed P(s) fit (log-log regression or loess over diagonals). IF FOUND: report sensitivity. Prefer a robust or smoothed expected (cooltools smooths P(s) by default), or one that excludes the target pixel, and state which was used. SOURCE: https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/cooltools/api/expected.html

sl-test-v2-e955b9b87a07.label: Pseudoreplication: model at donor level
sl-test-v2-e955b9b87a07.text: PITFALL: Cells from one donor are pseudoreplicates; genotype varies only between donors (24 donors, ~588 cells in cells.csv), so a cell-level GLM that treats cells as independent gives badly overconfident SEs and lets donors with many cells dominate beta. CHECK: count cells per donor and per genotype group within the activated subset; compare donor-level random-effect variance or pseudobulk vs naive cell-level fits. IF FOUND: estimate beta with a donor-level model: sum-pseudobulk counts per donor in the activated subset, fit NB/Poisson GLM count ~ g + covariates + offset(log summed total_umi) (offset-pseudobulk equals a GLMM in point estimate and SE), or use an NB GLMM with a donor random intercept (NEBULA/glmmTMB). Report the estimate on the natural-log scale per allele (g coded 0/1/2). SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-21038-1 ; https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/40/8/btae498/7730101

sl-test-v2-29af0e776371.label: per-replicate O/E then average
sl-test-v2-29af0e776371.text: PITFALL: Case and control replicates can differ in sequencing depth and distance-decay shape, so comparing raw counts or pooled matrices confounds depth or P(s) changes with loop changes. CHECK: compare total counts and log-log P(s) slopes across the 4 replicates (ctrl_r1, ctrl_r2, case_r1, case_r2). IF FOUND: compute expected within each replicate (O/E is self-normalizing for depth), compute log2(O/E) per replicate, then average across the 2 replicates per condition as the task defines. Do not sum replicates first unless you justify it. Report the spread between replicates. Consider joint normalization (multiHiCcompare loess) as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6069782/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11879411/

sl-test-v2-f649bf2ec3a0.label: Ambient RNA contamination of CXCL10
sl-test-v2-f649bf2ec3a0.text: PITFALL: Ambient (cell-free) RNA adds counts of highly expressed induced genes such as CXCL10/ISG15/IFI6 to every droplet, which inflates expression in low-expressing cells and shrinks (attenuates) genotype log rate ratios toward zero, or creates spurious ones if the ambient level differs by sample. CHECK: empty_drops.csv.gz gives ambient counts for barcodes with low total_umi; compute the ambient fraction of each gene (gene/total_umi in empty drops) and compare it with cell-level fractions; estimate contamination fraction rho using a gene that should be absent from monocytes (e.g. HBB) in the style of SoupX: rho ~ (HBB/total in cells)/(HBB/total in soup). Note that empty_drops has no donor column, so the ambient profile is pooled. IF FOUND: subtract expected ambient counts (rho * total_umi * ambient fraction) per cell before aggregation (SoupX-style), or include ambient expectation in the model, and report beta with and without correction as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7763177/ ; https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA.multisample/ambient-problems.html

sl-test-v2-86d31681aae2.label: mean of logs, pseudocounts
sl-test-v2-86d31681aae2.text: PITFALL: Mean of log2(O/E) across replicates differs from log2 of mean O/E, and zero counts give -inf. CHECK: look at the target pixel's count in each replicate and at any zeros on diagonal 9. IF FOUND: follow the task definition literally (compute log2 per replicate, then take the arithmetic mean). Use a pseudocount only if a zero occurs, and state it. Compute delta as the case mean minus the control mean. SOURCE: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GPTomics/bioSkills/main/hi-c-analysis/hic-visualization/SKILL.md

sl-test-v2-4d12ff7c83fc.label: Do not gate activated cells on CXCL10
sl-test-v2-4d12ff7c83fc.text: PITFALL: Double dipping and selection bias. If the activated subpopulation is defined by thresholding or clustering on CXCL10 itself (or on genes strongly correlated with it), the outcome is conditioned on, which truncates its distribution and biases the genotype effect (usually toward zero, and the direction can be unpredictable). CHECK: define activation only from markers other than CXCL10 (e.g. IFI6, ISG15, normalised by total_umi), and check how sensitive beta is to the threshold or mixture-model cutoff. IF FOUND: exclude CXCL10 from the gating; use a mixture model or a pre-specified rule on the other ISGs; consider data splitting or a soft (probabilistic) assignment weighting; report sensitivity across reasonable gates. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13692059/ ; https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(19)30269-8

sl-test-v2-760350702368.label: global vs local (donut) expected
sl-test-v2-760350702368.text: PITFALL: Global (diagonal) expected flags any pixel inside a domain as enriched. Loop callers (HiCCUPS/cooltools dots) compare against a local donut/lower-left background instead. CHECK: compute O/E for the 8-17 pixel against the donut neighbourhood (e.g. a ring of pixels 1-3 bins around it, excluding the peak row and column) and compare with the diagonal-expected O/E. IF FOUND: if the two diverge, report diagonal-expected O/E as the primary result (the task asks for observed/expected) and the local enrichment as QC. Say whether the change between conditions is a focal loop change or a broad domain change. SOURCE: https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/dots.html ; https://github.com/XiaoTaoWang/HiCPeaks

sl-test-v2-c23b56ee1641.label: State-specific effect vs composition
sl-test-v2-c23b56ee1641.text: PITFALL: State-specific eQTL vs composition. Genotype can change the FRACTION of monocytes that are activated, not only CXCL10 per activated cell; an estimate pooling all monocytes or using a mis-gated subset mixes the two effects, and the task asks for the within-activated-state effect. CHECK: tabulate the activated fraction per donor against g; fit the per-state model and also a genotype x state interaction model (count ~ g*state + offset, donor random effect). IF FOUND: report beta from the activated stratum (or the g coefficient + g:state interaction for activated) and not the pooled monocyte effect; describe the composition effect separately.
